entry.title: Rsa Julia
entry.content:
Julia

A few months back while talking with a coworker he mentioned he was prototyping one of our bidding projects in Julia as a way to address some of the performance issues with our current python implementation. That project didnt end up panning out for a couple of reasons, but what I saw of Julia impressed me. A staticly typed, compiled language, with the rich type inference and dead simple syntax of python? Add in native support for Nd matrices, and speed comparable to numpy or c/++/# and I knew I had to check this language out.

Pros

So far, I’ve been really happy working with Julia, especially compared to any other staticly typed, compiled language I worked with. Setup was a breeze - and the vscode extension is amazing. Julia works seamlessly with vscode’s jupyter tooling and the linting worked out of the box for me. Except for Python, Julia has easily has the best Jupyter support of any language I’ve worked with. Error messages are clear and to the point, the package manager is great, and the syntax is super simple and concise, comparable to python or go. But whereas the simplisitic syntax of python and go feels constricting, you can basically do whatever you want in Julia. I think a great example is how ternary operators are handled:

Look at how easily I can defer execution using chained ternary operators in julia:

f = () -> begin println("f"); false end
g = () -> begin println("g"); true end
h = () -> begin println("h"); true end

#69 (generic function with 1 method)

(true ? f() : g()) ? g() : h()

f
h



true

(false ? f() : g()) ? g() : h()

g
g



true

In contrast, pythons ternary equivalent not only looks ugly, but has unintuitive syntax and nesting. Although it supports short circuit evaluation, the order of execution is not very readable because the conditional is in the middle of the branching expressions. Note also that python does not support multi line lambdas - super annoying.

def f():
    print("f")
    return False
def g():
    print("g")
    return True
def h():
    print("h")
    return True

g() if (f() if True else g()) else h()

f
h





True

g() if (f() if False else g()) else h()

g
g





True

I think Julia is probably the closest to Javascript in terms of ease of use and functional programming support - but with the added benefit of a strict type system. Unlike Javascript, I dont find myself getting burned by some weird corner case of null handling or string conversion.

Cons

Unfortunately, like all languages, Julia has its flaws. The 1-based indexing is a bizarre choice and I find myself subtracting 1 from many index vars just to emulate 0-indexing - but given Julia is a scientific language it kindof makes sense that it would inherit some traits from Matlab. While I enjoy being able to define blocks and capture their end value w/ begin...end and being able to control scope w/ let...end, I dont like having type out multi character keywords all the time. I also think they interfere w/ the readability of the code if I follow patterns Im used to in javascript or c++. I miss the i++ and ++i operators - the equivalent block to i++ in julia is basically unusable: begin tmp = i; i += 1; tmp end.

I also find the OO elements of Julia a little clunky. Sometimes I want objects w/ member methods that have access to data scoped to that object. You can techincally use the JS function == object == class approach in Julia - but its clunky, the syntax is unintuitive, and linting doesnt work.

O = () -> begin
    size = 0
    li = (n) -> 2*n + 1
    ri = (n) -> 2*n + 2
    pi = (n) -> floor(Int,(n-1)/2)
    return () -> (size;li;ri;pi)
end
o = O()
o.li(1)
o.size

0

You can do something similar w/ classes having functions as member variables, but again, linting doesnt work and I get the feeling this just isnt how you are supposed to write Julia.

mutable struct DictHeap
	v        	::Array
	d        	::Dict
	size     	::Int
	priority	::Function
	li			::Function
	ri			::Function
	pi			::Function

	DictHeap(;priority=(el) -> el) = new(
		[],Dict(),0,
		priority,
		(n) -> 2*(n-1) + 1 + 1,
		(n) -> 2*(n-1) + 2 + 1,
		(n) -> floor(Int,(n-1-1)/2)+1
	)
end

Verdict

Overall, Julia rocks - I’d love to get some professional experience working w/ it.

RSA

Around the same time, an old college friend reached out to me for some help w/ one of those take home coding assignments. He

RSA

can find positive integers e,d,n s.t

(m^e)^d \congruent(n) m

(m^d)^e \congruent(n) m

public key is then n and e - private key is n and d - although only d is actually kept private

m is the encrpyed payload

Key gneeration

  1. chose prime #s p q - similarly sized ,larged, random - differ in len by a few digits
  2. n = pq - bits in n is the key length - as in rsa2556
  3. carmichael fn \lam, lam(n) = m smallest s.t. a^m % n = 1 \forall a coprime to n
    • \lam(n) = lcm(lam(p),lam(q))
      n = pq => a ^ \lam(n) % n = 1
      => a ^ \lam(p) = 1 % pq && a ^ \lam(q) = 1 % pq 
        1/pq = 1/p 
  (x / (pq)) % pq = x/p % pq * x/q % pq
  a ^ lcm(\lam(p),\lam(q)) % (pq) = a ^ s ^ \lam(p) % (pq) = a ^ t ^ \lam(q) % (pq) = 1
  a ^ s ^ \lam(p) / p * 1/q = (k + 1/p) * 1/q = (pk + 1)/pq
                                              = (lq + 1)/pq
  pk = lq => divisibnle by both p and q
                                              => % pq = 1
  any multiple of \lam(q) and \lam(p) will be congruent to 1 but lcm is lowest such
    • for all primes carmichaels totient \lam = eulers toitent \phi
    • for all primes eulers toitent = p-1
    • also Fermats little theorem 
        a^p \congruent(p) a
  a^(p-1) \congruent(p) 1
      • Proof:
        • consider dictionary of strings of length p w/ alphabet of size a
        • remove all strings completely composed of the same character - which is a
        • all remaining strings may be grouped by whether they are equal if ends are connected
        • these groups are of size p
        • so (a^p - a) % p = 0 => a^p /congruent(p) a
        • can divide both sides by a => a^(p-1) % p = 1
          • a^p % p = a % p
        • what if p|a? - in this case a^(p-1) % p = 0
        • what if a|p? a = 2 , p = 4 2 ^ (4-1) % 4 = 0
        • b/c common divisor of a,p is divisible by p when exponentiated enough
    • \lam(n) = lcm(\lam(p),\lam(q)) = lcm(p-1,q-1)
    • lcm computed used Euclidean algo -
      • lcm(m,n) = m * n / gcd(m,n)
  4. chose e s.t 1 < e < \lam(n) & gcd(e,\lam(n)) = 1 - i.e. coprime e and lam(n)
    • e should have a small bit length and hamming weight 3 smalest and fastest - but 2^16 + 1 is most common
    • e part of public key
  5. d is then d %=\lam(n) e^-1 - => de % \lam(n) = 1
    • d computed via Extended Euclidean Algo b/c e & \lam(n) comprime
    • d kept secret as private key exp

public key is then modulus n and public encryption exponent e - d is then the private decrpytion exponeent

p, q and \lam(n) can be kepy secret b/c they can be used to calcujlate d - but dont need to be remembered

NOTE: apparently eulers totient can be used instead of carmichaels - so (p-1)(q-1) works just as well as \lcm(p-1,q-1) - but this makes decription key larger than it need to be

NOTE: decryption key can be chosed before encryption key to make decryption eky smaller and faster

  • but modern algos prioritize encryption speed over decription key

Encryption

message m

encrypted payload = m ^ e % n

Decryption

payload ‘p = m^e % n`

p^d % n = m^e^d % n = m

NOTE Chinese remainder theorem used for decryption

Goal

Modular exponentiation is irreversable “1-way fn” - so if we can find e,d,n s.t. for any message integer m:

(m^e)^d = m % n

then we can encrypt m via modular exponentiation over n by e - n and e then form public (encryption) key

we can then decrypt this encrpyted message by modular exponentiation over n by d n and d then form private (decryption) key - although only d is kept private

Key generation

  1. choose 2 large primes p,q - differ in length by a few digits - random - large
  2. n = pq
  3. Want to find a k s.t for all m =====»> m^k = 1 % n
    • FLT:
      • for prime n - a^n - a = 0 mod n - for all a
        • alphabet of size a
        • universe of strings of length m => a^m = a && a^(m - 1) = 1 mod n && a^(n-2) = 1/a mod n 
           m^k = 1 % (pq)
 By FLT:
 m^(p-1) = 1 % p && m^(q-1) = 1 
 m^(p-1) % pq = (s*p + 1) % pq
 m^(q-1) % pq = (t*q + 1) % pq
 m^(p-1)(q-1) = (t*q + 1) % pq
   = (p*s + 1) % pq
   = (k*p*q / gcd(pq) + 1) % pq
   = 1

          So we have k = (p-1)(q-1) AND m^(p-1)(q-1) = 1 % pq NOTE - cant do m^((p-1)*(q-1)+1) % pq b/c that requires u to know m at decryption time!

  4. WTF e,d s.t. e*d = i*k + 1 where i is some int => e*d = 1 % k If we choose e prime < k ==» gcd(e,k) = 1 - then last step of Euclids gcd(e,k) is 
     ae + bk = gcd(e,k) = 1

    so a = d

    Can also use FLT b/c e,k coprime

     e^(k-1) = 1 % k
  = e * e^(k-2) = 1 % k
 d = e ^ (k-2) % k

Euclids:

x1*a + y1*b = gcd(a,b)
    = gcd(b,a%b)
    = x2*b + y2*a%b
    = x2*b + y2(a - a//b * b)
    = y2*a + (x2b - y2*b * a//b)
    = y2*a + (x2-y2*a//b)*b

Generating large primes

can do a deterministic sieve - but takes too long for large #s

instead do probabilistic tests

Fermat primality test

n prime , a pos int - a^(n-1) % n = 1

so we just have to find a val a s.t a^(n-1) % m != 1

this a fermat witness

Some #s satisfy Fermats little theroem for all vals of a - these are Carmichael #s

Only 255 Carmichael #s < 10^8 - so prob that tested # n is a carmichael # is very low

000 001 010 011 100 101 110 111

000 - 111 001 - 010 - 100 011 - 101 - 110

0000 - 1111 0001 - 0010 - 0100 - 1000 0011 - 0110 - 1100 - 1001 0101 - 1010 0111 - 1110 - 1101 - 1011

cyclic permutation proof only works a cyclic permutation must go full circle before repeating itself i.e. if pemutation lengt his prime

so Fermats primaility test can succeed for non primes

so a # satisfies Fermats primailty test if but not only if it is prime

p prime -> FPT

FPT -/> p prime

Miller Rabin

try to find non-trivial square roots of 1 modulo p

a^2 %p= 1
=> `a` non-trvial square root of %p= 1

- if exists `s` s.t.
a^2 = s*p + 1


using Primes
D = 256
small_primes = Primes.primes(1000)
gen_prime(d) = begin
    test_prime(p) = begin
        if any([(q^2 <= p && p % BigInt(q) == 0) for q in small_primes]) return false end
        return true
    end
    p = -1
    p = rand(BigInt(1)<<(d-1) : BigInt(1)<<d)
    p = Primes.nextprime(p,1)
    # for i in 1:1000

    return p
end

p = gen_prime(floor(Int,D/2)+8)
q = gen_prime(floor(Int,D/2)-8)
n = p*q
isprime(p),isprime(q)

egcd = (a,b) -> begin
    if b == 0 return (a,1,0) end
    g,x,y = egcd(b,a%b)
    return (g,y,x-y*floor(BigInt,a/b))
end
powmod = (a,b,c) -> b == 0 ? 1 : mod(((b&1)*(a-1)+1) * powmod(a,b>>1,c)^2,c)
phi = (p-1)*(q-1)
e = BigInt(1<<16 + 1) # 65537 - prime
d::BigInt
(_,d,_) = egcd(e,phi);
d += phi*ceil(Int,-d/phi)
# d = powmod(e,phi-2,phi)
mod(d*e,phi)
c = powmod(8,e,n)
c,powmod(c,d,n)

entry.summary: Julia A few months back while talking with a coworker he mentioned he was prototyping one of our bidding projects in Julia as a way to address some of the performance issues with our current python implementation. That project didnt end up panning out for a couple of reasons, but what I saw of Julia impressed me. A staticly typed, compiled language, with the rich type inference and dead simple syntax of python? Add in native support for Nd matrices, and speed comparable to numpy or c/++/# and I knew I had to check this language out.

entry.title: Beginnings
entry.content:
I recently - well - not that recently (about a year ago) - switched from a job where I worked 60+ hr weeks to one where I work a standard 40 hours. Since the company is EST and I live in PST, Im basically free after 2pm. Now that I have some time on my hands, Ive been taking my hobby projects a little more seriously. I’ve also brought some of my old projects back from the dead and given them a little facelift - namely my old Starcraft bot. Anyways - I think the time has come to start writing up some of these projects and showing them off.

I think Ill start by posting a quick writeup I did on my first experiences w/ the Julia language using it to code out an implementation of RSA from scratch. I will say - as I was writing that post - I found it getting a little long and unfocused. Does a reader really want to see my fumbling attempts at showing why optimizations like Carmichaels totient and the Chinese remainder theorem are useful and important? Is it really useful to explain Miller-Rabin? I think I might have to cut it down and may just focus on the basics of the algo and its goals. We’ll see.

I think next I’ll probably write up something on using powerful ML estimators like Xgboost or sklearns MLP implementation as a Kaplan Meier estimator for survival analysis. Its a problem that comes up surprisingly often, and I’ve found the already implemented algorithms in the excellent liflines package are too slow for the kind of rich datasets you encounter in a professional context.

After that …. I’m not sure. I made a fun little AI for the popular 2048 game to beat my brother’s high score. I think I finally understand alpha/beta pruning now - as well as the importance of a good hueristic function and why OpenAI used machine learning for their hueristics. Also I think an a post w/ an embedded widget of my AI autoplaying the game would be cool.

I also spent a lot of time working on a VR physics/animation engine for Babylon.js for an Avatar game. That project needs a ton of work though, and I actually had to stop working on it for a bit b/c I ran into a version conflict b/w the packages I was using. I’ll probably come back to it later, but to be honest I dont know when I could demo it on this blog.

I might write up an analysis of CDC vaccination and VAERS data I did after a discussion w/ a couple friends where I realized that it was difficult to find any objective hard analyses of effect size online. I do worry that by the time I get around to that writeup Ill have to redo all the work to incorporate the much larger amount of data gathered from then till now, and since I’m not a SME I just worry Ill make some kind of dumb mistake on a topic people care a lot about.

I may also revisit a topic I researched in college and have returned to off and on ever since. Every year EIA and Lazard publish LCOE #s for various power sources, and whenever they are discussed online I see a lot of confusion about how the numbers are calcuated and what they mean. I also see people posting a lot of #s from source specific orgs like IRENA and IAEA, and making all kinds of apples to oranges comparisons. I think I could do a ton of posts about either one of those topics, but I might just start out w/ a replication of LCOE #s and some discussion about input parameters and assumptions. Again, I wonder when Ill get around to this, for some reason its a charged subject and I dont want to make any mistake in my implementation.

Well - I think thats all I have for the forseeable future — looking forward to what I can get done by EOY.
entry.summary: I recently - well - not that recently (about a year ago) - switched from a job where I worked 60+ hr weeks to one where I work a standard 40 hours. Since the company is EST and I live in PST, Im basically free after 2pm. Now that I have some time on my hands, Ive been taking my hobby projects a little more seriously. I’ve also brought some of my old projects back from the dead and given them a little facelift - namely my old Starcraft bot. Anyways - I think the time has come to start writing up some of these projects and showing them off.
